text: Ministers have promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people as they gave their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report, promising spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals and giving him a government role to push them through. Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, spent more than two hours in the Commons taking questions on the report and Labour MPs were almost without exception positive or neutral; there was no evidence that Andy Burnham faces a significant backbench revolt any time soon. But some leftwingers are alarmed about the proposed cuts, which also concern disability groups. Frances Ryan has set out the case against in her Guardian column. Here is an extract.

double quotation markThis is in effect the creation of a two-tier welfare state, where the help you receive isn’t determined by your health but the date on your birth certificate. The £3.6bn in cuts would sever the link between need and entitlement that sits at the heart of the safety net – potentially leading to the perverse situation where two people with the same disability get unequal support simply because they’re a different age. After months of stories inflaming the narrative that feckless youngsters are feigning disability for cash, as a fashion statement or because of “social contagion”, Milburn will have felt under immense pressure to curb the youth benefits bill as a trade-off for his other large-scale spending plans. That pensioners receive roughly 55% of the welfare budget and young people (excluding children) just 2.5% is conveniently ignored.
And here is Frances’s column in full.

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.

Liberal Democrats have today been paying tribute to John Pardoe, the former Liberal deputy leader, who has died. Ed Davey described him as “one of that small band of MPs who kept the Liberal flame burning brightly in the 1960s and 70s”. Paul Walter has more in a post at Liberal Democrat Voice.
What disability and health charities are saying about Milburn report
Here is some reaction to the Milburn report from disability and health charities.
From Ross Barrett, senior policy manager at the MS Society

double quotation markProposals to create a new youth welfare system in place of personal independence payment (Pip) and the universal credit (UC) health element would likely mean some young people with MS losing financial support. This could be dangerous and ultimately counter-productive. Without Pip, young people will struggle to manage the overwhelming extra costs of the condition, face worsening health, and may find it harder to stay in work.
From a National Autistic Society spokesperson

double quotation markWe welcome the report’s calls for significant investment in earlier employment support and that there should be no changes to financial entitlements until that support is place. We also welcome the focus on driving down the disability employment gap, something we have been demanding for years. For Alan Milburn’s proposed system to be effective for autistic people, it will require a very high level of autism training and understanding for anyone supporting autistic young people or deciding what they are entitled to.
From Dr Sarah Hughes, CEO of Mind,

double quotation markEmployment support on its own isn’t enough - it needs to go hand in hand with an overhaul of mental health support. It’s hugely promising to see such a clear ambition to better tailor mental health support through an open access approach that Mind has been calling for. This means that young people will be able to get support they need, on the day they need it, enabling them to get into work. “But building a bridge to employment won’t work without an adequate benefits safety net. We’re concerned that young people with mental health problems could be left scrambling desperately to make ends meet, so we must see clear evidence that benefits will meet their essential costs. Without this, these changes could worsen mental health, make it harder to engage with support and push our young people further into the cold.
From Simon Antrobus, CEO at the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB)

double quotation markYoung people with visual impairment are twice as likely to be NEET than their peers. There is clear ambition to raise the bar of opportunity for disabled young people to pursue the careers they want. But we will only achieve the seismic change we all want to see if support is shaped by specialists who understand the unique needs and societal barriers faced by disabled young people, including those with vision impairment.
Burnham delays announcement about options for closer relationship with EU until next month
Andy Burnham has delayed his announcement about the possible options for Britain forming a closer relationship with the EU after the next election.

At Labour conference in September, Burnham said that he wanted to open a national debate on this topic, indicating that joining the customs union or the single market, or even rejoining in full, were all potential options that could be put to the public in Labour’s next manifesto.

In recent weeks, No 10 has been saying that Burnham would do this around the time of the UK-EU summit taking place that is taking place on Friday – implying soon afterwards. Whether his intervention would take the form of a speech, or a statement to MPs, or the publication of a document has not been specified.

But, in his interview with Sky’s Beth Rigby, Burnham said he was now planning to set this all out alongside his 10-year plan, “next month”. He has said the 10-year plan will be published before the Commons rises for the Christmas recess on Thursday 17 December.

double quotation markI’m in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal. That’s what I’m doing this week [at the summit]. We’ll see how it goes. And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. And I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.
Burnham also insisted there was no rush.
double quotation markAll I’m going to do is look at what options might be available, so that people can see the pros and cons, but [I] will set those out, in due course. There’s no rush to do that.
When it was put to him that Boris Johnson said it would be madness to reopen the debate about the UK being a member of the EU, Burnham replied:

double quotation markI’m afraid I’m not going to listen to Boris Johnson on this particular matter. He burnt bridges and created a lot of bad feeling. And consequently Britain has suffered as a result of that.
Burnham says government departments will have to find savings to fund new Youth Opportunity Service
Andy Burnham has recorded an interview with Beth Rigby from Sky News to mark the publication of the Alan Milburn review. Here are the top lines on this topic.
Burnham described the publication of the Milburn report as a “watershed moment” for Britain. He said:

double quotation markLet’s first be clear what this is. It’s a watershed moment. I said to the cabinet this morning, I don’t think a British cabinet has sat around that table in 50 years or more and talked about a vision for young people, support from the very early years all the way through school and then into opportunity beyond school. And that’s what this is about.
He did not rule out implementing the Milburn recommendation to cut employer national insurance for young people. (See 3.38pm.) Asked if he would accept this idea, he replied:

double quotation markWe’re going to look at the whole of the report in the round. Some of the implications of those proposals are for the budget, and they’ll have to be considered as part of that. But we’re not ruling anything out at this point in time. We’ll look at everything in the round.

He confirmed that government departments will be asked to make cuts in some areas to free up funds for the Youth Opportunity Service being set up. (See 1.33pm.) Asked if benefits were being cut to fund better employment support, Burnham said:

double quotation markNo. That’s not the approach that we’ll be taking. I am asking the cabinet to reprioritise. That’s the discussion that I’ve been having. So Department for Education, Work and Pensions, Health and Social Care – finding money now, to put in place the first budget for the Youth Opportunity Service next year.
This is what the Milburn report says about what the new Youth Opportunity Service should do.

double quotation markA new Youth Opportunity Service (YOS) should operate in every part of England as the delivery mechanism for these Guarantees. Its purpose should be to make sure that a young person who is outside education or work, or at serious risk of becoming so, has somewhere to go and somebody responsible for helping them move forward. Access to the YOS should depend on a young person’s need for help, not on whether they happen to be claiming benefits. It should be easy to find, welcoming and non-stigmatising, whether a young person reaches it online, through a physical service or through an organisation they already know and trust. It should identify young people before detachment becomes entrenched, help them find jobs, apprenticeships, courses, work experience and other opportunities, understand what is getting in the way and, where more sustained help is needed, bring together one Participation Plan and one named relationship around the young person. It should operationalise the new welfare and benefits system for young people.
Milburn said an initial £500m should be spent setting up the service in 2027.
Bev Craig says she wants to see Manchester implementing Milburn's plans for tackling Neets within 12 months
Josh Halliday is the Guardian’s North of England editor.

Andy Burnham’s successor as Greater Manchester mayor, Bev Craig, said she wants to implement Alan Milburn’s model for tackling the Neets crisis “within 12 months,” describing the current system as “simply not acceptable”.
England’s mayors would be responsible for huge parts of the proposals to get hundreds of thousands of young people earning or learning under plans set out by Milburn on Tuesday.

Among sweeping changes to health and skills programmes, the mayors of strategic authorities would be responsible for getting young people into work or education up to the age of 24 – which Milburn’s report describes as a “fundamental change” from the current system where teenagers hit a “cliff edge” of state support as soon as they reach 19.

A new funding settlement would see the more established authorities - like Greater London, Greater Manchester and South Yorkshire - given committed pots of cash for at least three years to replace the rolling annual grants they receive from central government.
Mayors whose areas underperform in getting young people into work would face financial penalties as part of this model.

Speaking to the Guardian, Craig said her predecessor Burnham now had a “moral imperative in acting fast” on Milburn’s recommendations – and said Greater Manchester should be at the front of the queue for these new responsibilities.

Asked whether she was concerned about Milburn’s proposed cuts to disability benefits for young people, which by 2036/7 would amount to £3.6bn a year, Craig said that was “not my reading of the 278-page report”.

double quotation markThere naturally will be a debate on social security that will move through parliament, but my takeaway from this report is that we’ve got a generation of young people who want to work and want to get into education, who currently aren’t supported to be able to do that.

Craig said the status quo was “simply not acceptable” and that nearly 40,000 young people in Greater Manchester were neither earning or learning. According to the Centre for Cities thinktank, Manchester has the third highest number of young Neets in England behind London and Birmingham - although this is not particularly surprising given the size of these cities.
Here are comments on the Milburn report from education unions.
From Matt Wrack, general secretary of the NASUWT, a teachers’ union

double quotation markWe reject any approach to getting young people into employment, education and training which is based on punitive cuts to welfare or which seeks to blame schools or teachers. Young people should not be penalised for the wider and prolonged failures of successive governments to create high quality training opportunities, invest in decent jobs and to create the social conditions in which young people can thrive and feel hope for the future.
From Paul Whiteman, general secretary at the school leaders’ union NAHT

double quotation markWe welcome the recognition that young people should have an education system which prepares them not only for exams, but for adult life, further study and employment. NAHT has long supported a broad and balanced curriculum, alongside greater parity of esteem between academic, vocational and technical pathways, so that every young person can pursue a route that reflects their talents, strengths and aspirations.
From Jo Grady, general secretary of the UCU, which represents academics

double quotation markCreating tens of thousands of new jobs in further education would be a welcome step towards tackling youth unemployment. But the government cannot expect colleges to deliver this ambition while presiding over a further education workforce crisis.
Scottish government says it's doing 'many' of ideas Milburn recommends already

The Scottish government has said that “many” of the reforms proposed by Alan Milburn are already being implemented north of the border. In a statement, the Scottish government’s education secretary, Màiri McAllan, said:

double quotation markWe will take time to consider Alan Milburn’s report in detail. We are so ambitious for our young people, who face unique challenges in today’s economy, having grown up in the nearly 20 years since the global financial crash, through years of Westminster austerity and the economic and social catastrophe of Brexit. Where there is opportunity to collaborate with the UK Government and others for the benefit of young people in Scotland, we will take it. However, many of the reforms it recommends for England – including stronger vocational curriculum and qualifications, tracking of young people’s activity and joined up support wrapped around them to help them participate – reflect approaches Scotland has already embedded over many years … Alan Milburn’s interim report notes there are around 40% of 16 to 19-year olds starting an apprenticeship, compared with around 20% of 16 to 18-year olds in England. In Scotland, 95.7% of school leavers are in a positive destination three months after leaving school, the joint second highest on record. For 16-24 year olds, the employment rate is higher in Scotland than in England, and the majority of our economically inactive young people are students.
Brian Leishman was probably the Labour MP most critical of the Milburn plans during the Common statement. He said:

double quotation markThe Milburn Review will consign some people into destitution – the author himself said that it won’t be pain-free. How can we think that withdrawing benefits from disabled people and putting them into poverty is acceptable?
In response, Pat McFadden said: “It is a life on benefits that leaves people in poverty.”
Funding tax cuts 'difficult', says McFadden, when asked about Milburn's national insurance proposals

In the Commons, Pat McFadden sidestepped a question from Oliver Dowden about whether the government would implement Alan Milburn’s recommendation for a cut in employer national insurance for young people. (See 2.06pm.) But, when the Labour MP Jonathan Brash asked if ministers would accept this proposals, McFadden gave a more direct reply. Arguing that tax was a matter for the chancellor, he said:

double quotation markThere is already a break in the system for employers with regard to employees under the age of 21. I’m sure the chancellor listens to all representations about tax but he has the difficult job of netting off all these representations whenever there is a fiscal event.
This is what the Milburn report says about cutting national insurance.

double quotation markWhile structural reductions in employment taxation cannot be delivered immediately, that should not prevent government from setting a clear direction towards lower payroll taxes. Rather than across the board, poorly targeted and unaffordable cuts in employer national insurance, I propose a different course: targeted support now, followed by a 5-year glide path to lower national insurance costs for workers aged 21 to 24. Businesses need confidence that government’s ambition is to reduce, not continually increase, the cost of employing a young person. A start should be made with the 2 sectors which provide the most entry level jobs for young people: retail and hospitality. When fiscal conditions allow, the point at which employers in those sectors pay employer national insurance for 21 to 24 year-olds should double and rise progressively from the current £5,000 threshold to a new one of £10,000. Before the 2025 changes that threshold was £9,100. Unlike a full or partial employer national insurance exemption for 21 to 24 year-olds, increasing the threshold would have the biggest impact on the costs of recruiting low paid young workers and those who work fewer hours. It would especially help employers recruit young people doing ‘Saturday jobs’ as once the threshold reaches £10,000, a 21 year-old could work 15 hours a week at current minimum wage rates without the employer paying any employer national insurance. Over time the government should consider how to extend this new employer national insurance relief to other sectors in the economy, focusing on those with the biggest potential to create more entry level jobs for the young.
